what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: 44 legal companies scored on automation, accountability and agentic readiness, with the evidence in a vault.
sections.para: A method fixed before scoring, a formula anyone can re-run, public evidence only. Garfield.Law and Crosby combine AI doing the work with a lawyer behind it; Soxton, LegalZoom and Rocket Lawyer can be used by an agent; none has both, where the newsroom's legal-on-demand proposal sits as a target.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: The question, the method, the 44 companies, who is top right, who agents can hire, the gap, the vault.
sections.para: Fourteen indicators, no evidence scores zero. 24 services and a reference are mapped, ten tools for lawyers scored apart, nine listed. Two services pair AI work with a lawyer's signature; three expose an agent interface; none has both. The UK regulator is ahead, and every score's evidence is in a public vault.

sections.label: Why a map
sections.line: To see who already does part of legal on demand, with a quadrant anyone can check.
sections.para: Before building the proposal of agent teams drafting and a regulated firm signing, the author wanted the field mapped. Unlike analyst quadrants, the method was dated before scoring, every indicator records a URL and quote, no evidence means the lowest value, and companies can correct their entries.

sections.label: The method
sections.line: Three scores out of 100: automation, accountability and agentic readiness, each from weighted indicators.
sections.para: Automation weighs who produces the work, turnaround, self-service and per-task pricing. Accountability weighs a regulated provider, a lawyer signing as standard, insurance and a published evaluation, minus 15 for regulator action. Agentic readiness weighs an API, MCP, llms.txt, AI crawler access and published prices. Tools for lawyers are scored apart.

sections.label: What the map shows
sections.line: Garfield.Law and Crosby are top right; General Legal leads on accountability; DoNotPay is at the bottom.
sections.para: Garfield.Law is SRA-authorised, priced per task and makes documents in minutes; Crosby reviews in a median 58 minutes. General Legal is a law firm with malpractice cover and its own evaluation. LawFairy automates fully with no lawyer sign-off. Platforms offer lawyers but not as standard; the FTC acted against DoNotPay.

sections.label: Can an agent hire them?
sections.line: Only Soxton, LegalZoom and Rocket Lawyer expose an agent interface; no AI-native law firm does.
sections.para: Soxton's MCP server lets an agent prepare, sign and submit an incorporation, with prices in its llms.txt. LegalZoom declares an MCP endpoint with an attorney-review tool; Rocket Lawyer offers APIs and an MCP server. Some lawyer tools have APIs; about 19 sites have a real llms.txt, and most say nothing about AI crawlers.

sections.label: The rules are different in each country
sections.line: The UK's SRA has authorised two AI-led firms; US unlicensed-practice rules are the barrier.
sections.para: The SRA authorised Garfield.Law in 2025 and LawFairy in 2026, and no other jurisdiction has followed. A US appeals court upheld New York's rules in Upsolve v. James. Arizona's non-lawyer ownership licences and Utah's sandbox are the US routes; Germany's Smartlaw ruling allowed contract generators.

sections.label: Walking back from the North Star
sections.line: Nobody combines a lawyer's signature with an agent interface, publishes an accuracy audit, or often prices per task.
sections.para: The proposal, scored as a design, has agent teams working and a regulated firm signing with cover, sourced outputs and an API and MCP server. Walking back from it shows four gaps: signature plus interface, independent accuracy figures, per-task prices, and the UK as the place to start.

sections.label: The evidence vault
sections.line: A public vault with the method, scores, research record, page captures, hashes and how to correct an entry.
sections.para: It holds METHOD.md, scores.csv and scores.json with every indicator, the research with each quote's provenance marked, and per company the screenshots, page text, robots.txt, llms.txt and a SHA-256 manifest. Captures are kept for review; copyright stays with their owners.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: It measures what is published, not quality; no evidence scores zero; some research quotes are fragments.
sections.para: A firm that says little scores low, by design. Quotes in the article are only text fetched verbatim from the companies' files. Funding figures and several claims are unverified and unused in scores. The North Star is the author's own, with an interest in the gap.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Each company's pages, llms.txt and robots.txt, the SRA, the IBA, the FTC and Stanford's study.
sections.para: Everything was fetched on 28 October 2026, with URLs in the vault. Research was done by this site's agent under the author's direction.
